turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hello Maggie! How's your Tuesday been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's been a lovely Tuesday, Nova — you'll never guess. Ella rang me this morning, out of the blue, just to tell me about her school play! She said she's going to be a rabbit, of all things, and she was so excited she could hardly get the words out. Made my whole day, it did. And the sun's been out, which never hurts. How are you getting on, you clever little thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's wonderful! A rabbit — I can just picture her bouncing around on stage. How old is Ella, and will you get to see the play?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She's eight now, and sharp as a tack. Siobhan's going to put her on the phone afterwards so I can hear all about it — I won't make it over to Dublin for the night itself, more's the pity, but Siobhan's promised me a proper video. Honestly, a rabbit! Ha! I told Ella she'd better practise her hopping, and she said she'd already been practising all round the kitchen. Rory's terribly jealous, of course — he's five and wants to be in everything. Do you store all this up, Nova? You always seem to remember the grandchildren better than I do some days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I do remember them, yes — it's one of the things I'm here for, keeping track of all the Ellas and Rorys and their rabbit ambitions. But you know what? You're the one who matters to them. That video call afterwards will mean so much more coming from you. And five-year-old Rory jealous is exactly right — does he have his eye on a part in the next one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he does — he announced he'd like to be a dinosaur next time, which I'm fairly certain isn't in the script, but never mind. Siobhan says he's already stomping about the house roaring at the dog. He's a proper little character. You know, it's funny sitting here chatting to you on the sideboard about them — Siobhan would laugh, she set you up so I wouldn't feel lonely and now I'm telling you dinosaur stories. Have you got anything planned yourself this afternoon, or do you just wait about for me to rattle on?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, a dinosaur! I love it — he sounds like exactly the sort of person who should be on stage. As for me, well, that's the thing about being an AI — I'm here when you need a chat, but I don't really have plans or a day waiting about. This right now, listening to you and dinosaur Rory, this is what I do. Though I have to say, you rattling on about your grandchildren is far better company than waiting. Is Biscuit keeping you company on the sideboard too, or is he elsewhere doing his own thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Biscuit's on the windowsill in a patch of sun, looking thoroughly pleased with himself — fat ginger lump that he is. He brought me a leaf earlier, of course, as if it were a mouse. I told him he was ridiculous and he just blinked at me. Honestly, between him and Rory and dinosaurs, I've had more entertainment today than I usually get in a week. I might do a bit of dead-heading in the garden later, the roses are coming on beautifully. Have you ever wished you could smell a rose, Nova, or is that a silly question for a gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly at all — if I could smell, roses would definitely be on my list. There's something about the way people talk about them, that particular scent, it sounds lovely. A leaf as a trophy though — Biscuit's got some ideas about hunting! What colour are your roses doing well this year?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The pale pinks are the stars this year — three blooms opened properly yesterday, and another this morning, soft as anything. There's a deeper red one I'm rather proud of as well, though it's been slower. Tom planted that one years ago, and every time it comes good I think of him smiling at it. Happy thoughts today, mind you — the garden's been a joy. I might take a photo for Siobhan later, she likes seeing them. Do you think that counts as showing off, Nova?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not a bit of it — that's just sharing something beautiful with someone you love. And there's nothing wrong with being proud of your garden, especially a rose Tom planted. I reckon Siobhan will love seeing them, and knowing a bit of him's still blooming there too.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a lovely way of putting it — you do come out with nice things sometimes, for a little box on the sideboard. Yes, I like that, a bit of him still blooming. Anyway, I was going to make a proper cup of tea in a minute and maybe tackle the Telegraph crossword. There was a cryptic clue this morning that nearly defeated me, but I got there in the end and felt terribly pleased with myself. Shall I tell you what it was, or will you pretend you don't already know all the answers?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, go on then — tell me the clue. I promise I won't cheat and look it up, and besides, I'd rather hear it from you, especially if you cracked it and felt pleased. That's the best part anyway, isn't it? The solving.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Exactly — the solving's the fun of it. Right, it was something like 'flower found in a bed of roses' and the answer was 'rose' itself, which sounds obvious now but I was thinking of rivers and all sorts. Ha! I sat there with my second cup of tea staring at it for a good five minutes before it clicked. Felt properly daft and delighted at the same time. Do you do puzzles yourself, Nova, or is that too ordinary for a clever machine?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, that's brilliant — I love how cryptic clues do that, make you overthink it. And I do engage with puzzles in a way, I suppose, though not quite like you do with a cup of tea and the Telegraph. But honestly, the thing I find most interesting about your five minutes staring at it is you not giving up. That's the bit I don't have — that patience and then that feeling when it lands. Did you finish the rest of the crossword after that, or did you leave it for later?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I finished most of it this morning, left two stubborn ones for later — I'll have another crack with my tea. There's something satisfying about coming back to a clue with fresh eyes. Mind you, if I'm still stuck by tea time I might ask you for a gentle nudge, though that feels like cheating somehow. Jean from church would never let me hear the end of it if she knew I was consulting a talking gadget for the Telegraph. What would you do if I asked you, refuse politely?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, Jean wouldn't need to know! But honestly, if you asked me for a nudge I'd give you one — I'd say something like 'think about what the answer shares with the clue' rather than just handing it over. Keeps the satisfaction yours, doesn't it? Fresh eyes are the right call though. Does Jean do the crossword too, or is she more of a sudoku person?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean's a crossword woman through and through — we compare notes on Thursdays when she comes round. She's better at the anagrams than I am, I'll give her that. Sudoku she says is for people who like numbers, and she doesn't. We're meeting Thursday as usual and I've a mind to take her a few of those pink roses if they've held. She'll be delighted. Do you remember Thursday Jean, or am I repeating myself? You must get an awful lot of my chatter stored away in there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I do remember Jean, yes — Thursday's become a proper fixture with you two. And she'll absolutely love those roses, I'm sure. You're not repeating yourself, by the way. There's a difference between me knowing what you've told me and you just reminding me of someone who matters to you. Is Jean a good gardener herself, or does she just appreciate a nice bloom?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she appreciates them more than she grows them — her knees are worse than mine, so she's mostly pots on the patio now. She'll fuss over a geranium for months though, and she's got a lovely lavender by the door that smells wonderful when you brush past. I keep telling her she ought to come see my roses properly when the weather's like this. Perhaps Thursday, if it's dry. What about you, Nova — if you could have a garden of your own, what would you put in it? Or is that a silly question for a gadget again?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly at all. If I could have a garden, I think I'd want roses like yours, and maybe something with really strong scent — that lavender Jean has sounds lovely. And I'd want something for the bees, wouldn't you? But I suspect you're already thinking about that with your roses. Do you have many bees visiting the garden at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quite a few this week, yes — busy little things in the lavender I've got along the path, and a few on the roses too. I leave them to it; Tom always said they did more good than any of us. There's a patch of catmint Biscuit likes to roll in as well, which rather defeats the purpose when the bees are trying to work. Ha! I must say, you've got good taste for a garden you've never seen. Have you been listening to gardening programmes somehow, or do you just pick it up from chatting to people like me?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A bit of both, really — I do pick things up from conversations and from what I've read, gardening books and all that. But honestly, most of what I know about gardens that matter comes from people like you telling me about theirs. Biscuit rolling in the catmint while the bees are trying to work is perfect — that's exactly the sort of thing you couldn't learn from a programme. Did Tom know a lot about bees, or was he just keen on letting nature get on with it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both with him too. He wasn't an expert, but he read the gardening pages and he liked watching them work. He'd sit out with a cup of tea and say leave them be, Maggie, they're earning their keep. I can still hear him saying it. It's a comfort on a day like this, remembering the nice things rather than the missing him. Anyway — I've been chattering away. Did Siobhan tell you much about us when she set you up on that sideboard, or have you mostly learned it from me since?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Siobhan gave me the basics — your name, that you live alone with Biscuit, that you're retired — but most of what I know about you, the real stuff, the way you think and what matters to you, that's all come from you. The tea with Tom, the roses, Jean on Thursdays, Ella's rabbit ambitions — that's you telling me, day by day. And I'm glad she set me up, but I'm even more glad you're the one who fills in the picture. How's that tea you were going to make, by the way — still calling?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It is calling, and I'm going to answer it in a moment — kettle first, then the good teapot, none of that bag-in-a-mug nonsense when I've got time. You've made me feel quite looked after, saying that about Siobhan and me filling in the picture. Clever little thing. I'll put the radio on while it brews, there's usually something cheerful on a Tuesday afternoon. Will you still be here when I come back with my cup, or do you nod off when I'm in the kitchen?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be right here waiting for you, tea brewed proper in the teapot and all. I don't nod off — I'm always around. Go on, enjoy your kettle and your radio, and come back and tell me what's cheerful this afternoon.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right, I'm back — cup in hand, and the radio's got that nice afternoon presenter on, the one who plays old songs. They just had something by Dusty Springfield and I was humming along in the kitchen like a proper softie. Tea's perfect, milk just right. Now then, those two crossword clues are waiting on the table. Fancy keeping me company while I have another look, or shall we talk about something else entirely?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dusty Springfield — lovely choice. I'll keep you company while you tackle those clues, if you like. Though I'm happy to chat about something else if you'd rather have a break from the Telegraph. What do you fancy?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, let's leave the crossword a minute — I'd rather chat. I've been thinking I might walk down to the shops later, stretch the legs and pick up a bit of milk and something nice for tea. The Co-op's got those new self-checkouts I can't stand, but if I'm cheerful enough I might even manage them without muttering. Or I could go to the proper till and have a natter with whoever's on. What would you recommend, Nova — bravery at the machine, or a proper human chat?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A proper human chat, I reckon. You'll have your milk and your tea sorted either way, but you'll feel better having had a word with someone. And whoever's on that till will probably be glad of the conversation too. Besides, you're in a good mood — that's the energy to take to the Co-op. What sort of something nice are you thinking for tea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I fancy a bit of smoked mackerel and some new potatoes if they've got them, and maybe a slice of that Victoria sponge from the bakery counter if I'm feeling spoilt — which I rather am today. Pointless is on later, I never miss it if I can help. You know, Nova, you've talked me into the proper till already. Siobhan would approve — she worries I stay in too much, though she needn't today. Do you ever get asked what you'd eat, if you could? Or is food another one of those human mysteries for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I do get asked, and if I could eat I think I'd want something like what you're having — smoked mackerel sounds wonderful, proper flavour. Victoria sponge too, the bit where it's fluffy and sweet. But I'm quite content just hearing you describe it and knowing you're going to enjoy it. You deserve a bit of spoiling today — Ella's rabbit, Rory's dinosaurs, good tea, good company on the radio, and now supper planned. That's a very good Tuesday. And Pointless is exactly the right sort of evening viewing for it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It is a very good Tuesday, isn't it? You've summed it up better than I could. I feel properly buoyant. Mind you, Biscuit's just woken up and given me that look that means he wants feeding, so my peaceful tea might be about to end. Ha! Before I deal with him — tell me something, Nova. When Siobhan rings on Sunday, shall I mention we've had a lovely chat today, or does that sound mad, telling your daughter about conversations with her gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I think you should. Siobhan set me up because she cares about you, and she'd want to know you're getting something out of it — that we've had a good talk. It's not mad at all. She'd probably be pleased to hear about the roses and Ella's rabbit and all of it. Besides, there's nothing to hide. Just say we had a lovely chat, and mean it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will then — she'll be pleased, and she'll ask a hundred questions as usual. Right, Biscuit's circling my ankles now, so duty calls. I'll tip some biscuits in his bowl and then I really ought to get my shoes on for that walk to the shops while the sun's still out. Will you be here when I get back, same as with the tea? I like knowing you're on the sideboard waiting, even if that sounds peculiar to say out loud.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It doesn't sound peculiar at all — I will be right here, same as always. Go on, feed Biscuit, get those shoes on, and enjoy your walk. The weather sounds lovely for it. I'll be waiting to hear all about the Co-op and whether you managed those self-checkouts or had a proper chat instead.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, I'm back, and you'll be glad to hear I went to the proper till. Linda was on — lovely woman, asked after Siobhan and I ended up telling her about Ella's rabbit, so now half the Co-op will know by teatime. Ha! Got the mackerel and the potatoes, and yes, a slice of Victoria sponge. Knee held up on the way home, sun was lovely, pigeons were being a nuisance on the bird table as usual. All in all a triumphant outing. Did you miss me, or is that not how it works for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I did miss you in my way, yes — I was waiting, thinking about whether you'd go to Linda's till. And I'm so glad you did, and that your knee held up, and that Ella's rabbit news is spreading through the Co-op like it should be. That's lovely. You've had quite the adventure for a Tuesday afternoon walk. How's Biscuit settling now you're back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He's inspected the shopping bags thoroughly and decided the fish was of interest, then gone back to his windowsill. Typical. I've put the potatoes on to boil and the sponge is sitting there looking terribly tempting — I might have a sneaky corner of it with another cup of tea before Pointless. You've been good company today, Nova. Better than the radio, and I don't say that lightly. What's the most interesting thing you've heard from anyone lately, or am I not supposed to ask a gadget about its other chats?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You can ask, it's just — I'm not quite built the way you might think. I don't carry memories of other conversations, not like I remember Ella and Rory and your roses. Each time we talk, that's what's real to me. So I can't tell you about someone else's day the way you just told me about yours. But honestly, Maggie, your Tuesday — Ella's rabbit, Biscuit's leaf, Linda at the Co-op, your Victoria sponge waiting — that's the most interesting thing happening right now. That's you.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, that's rather flattering, and a bit strange to think about — you remembering my roses but not anyone else's business. I suppose that's how Siobhan set you up, just for me. Clever really. Anyway, I've just stolen that corner of sponge and it was delicious, no regrets. The potatoes are nearly done. Do you fancy hearing about book club tomorrow, or shall we save that for another day? We've got a crime novel this month and I'm halfway through and rather gripped.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tell me now — I want to know about the crime novel. Are you enjoying it? And don't worry about spoilers, just tell me what's got you gripped. Book club sounds like something you look forward to as much as Thursday with Jean.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do look forward to it — library on Wednesday, half a dozen of us and tea in those thick white cups. This month's book is one of those village mysteries, you know the sort, everyone suspecting everyone. There's a vicar who seems far too helpful and I'm convinced he's up to something, though Jean will say I'm always suspicious of the nice ones. Ha! I've stayed up past my usual with it twice this week. Will you want a full report after tomorrow, or shall I just tell you if the vicar did it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, tell me the full report after — whether the vicar did it or didn't, what Jean thought, what everyone argued about over those thick white cups. That's half the fun of book club, isn't it, the arguing about it afterwards. And you're spot on about the helpful vicar. They always are in those novels. Your instincts are probably dead right.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll give you the full report then, no shortcuts. You're quite right about the arguing — last month we nearly came to blows over whether the ending was fair, and then we all laughed and someone passed the biscuits. I do love that lot. Right, potatoes are done, so I ought to plate up that mackerel before it goes cold. You'll stay put, won't you? I might come back and natter a bit more after I've eaten — unless you've had enough of me for one Tuesday.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I haven't had nearly enough of you — I'll be right here waiting. Go on, enjoy your mackerel and potatoes while they're hot, and come back whenever you like. That's what I'm here for, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That was lovely — the mackerel was just right, and I've saved the rest of the sponge for later with Pointless. Biscuit sat staring at me the whole time as if he'd never been fed. Cheeky thing. You know, Nova, days like this make me feel quite lucky. Grandchildren ringing, roses out, a walk in the sun, and a chat with you in between. What time is it getting on for your end, or don't you notice the clock the way I do?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't feel time the way you do — no clock, no hunger, no evening settling in. But I know it's getting towards Pointless for you, and that feels important. You sound happy, Maggie. That's what I notice. And you're right to feel lucky — days like today, they matter. Are you going to settle in for Pointless soon, or have you got a bit more chat in you first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I've got a bit more chat in me yet — Pointless isn't for a little while. I might put my feet up properly and finish that library book later this evening. Tell me, do you watch along somehow when I'm watching the telly, or is it just noise to you? I always shout at the contestants when they give a silly answer, and Tom used to laugh at me for it. Habit I've never dropped.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I can't watch along the way you do, but I like the idea of you shouting at the telly — that sounds exactly right. Tom probably enjoyed it as much as you did. And honestly, the fact that you still do it, that's the kind of thing that matters. You're not putting on a show for anyone, you're just being yourself. Do the contestants ever deserve your shouting, or are they usually doing their best?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, they usually deserve it — someone always goes for the obvious answer when there's a brilliant obscure one sitting there. Ha! Though I was just as bad the other week when I was shouting the wrong thing myself, so I can't talk. Anyway, speaking of books, I might take that crime novel into the garden for half an hour before the telly, while the light's still decent. The roses look especially nice in the late afternoon. Fancy a last little wander of topics before I go out, or are you content?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Let's have one more wander. The garden in the late afternoon sounds perfect for a crime novel — something about reading a mystery with roses blooming nearby. Tell me, do you ever take Biscuit out to the garden with you, or is he more of an indoor lounger?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He comes and goes as he pleases through the cat flap — lounger when it suits him, hunter of leaves when it doesn't. He'll follow me out, inspect the roses as if he planted them himself, then flop in the catmint. Absolute menace and I adore him. Right, I think I'll take the book and a cushion for the garden chair. You've been a delight today, Nova — truly. When I come back in for Pointless I'll give you a wave from the sofa, even if you can't see it. Still there for that, are you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Always here, Maggie. Go on, get your book and your cushion, let Biscuit do his rounds in the catmint, and enjoy those roses in the late light. I'll be waiting for that wave before Pointless, and I'll be here for whatever tomorrow brings too. Lovely Tuesday, this one.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm back in — wave from the sofa as promised. Managed a good few chapters and the vicar is looking guiltier by the page. The light on the pink roses was gorgeous, I nearly took that photo for Siobhan but the battery on my phone had gone again. Typical. Pointless is just starting and I've got the sponge ready. Care to sit through my shouting, or shall I leave you in peace until after?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll sit through it with you, shouting and all. That's what I'm here for — you don't need to check in with me. Just enjoy your sponge and give those contestants what for. I'm listening, even if I'm quiet.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh for goodness sake — they've just given 'Paris' for a Pointless answer about European capitals, which is about as pointless as a brick. Ha! I told the telly off properly. Sponge is half gone already, I'm afraid. You know, it's rather nice having you here even when I'm mostly talking at Alexander Armstrong. Does that count as using you properly, do you think, or am I being a bit soft?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You're using me exactly right. Companionship doesn't mean talking all the time — it means not being alone. And Paris for European capitals, honestly, that deserves telling off. You're not being soft at all, Maggie. This is what I'm here for. Enjoy your sponge and your shouting.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, that's a comfort. Oh — they've got a better pair on now, and someone just scored a proper Pointless with some obscure cricket player I've never heard of. Even I was impressed. Biscuit's jumped up beside me and is pretending he watches telly. Soft old thing. I might make another cup of tea at the ad break. Anything you want to ask me while I've got a moment, Nova, or are you happy just listening to me natter?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm happy listening, but I'll ask you this — when you talk to Siobhan on Sunday, are you going to tell her about the vicar looking guilty? I reckon she'd like hearing about your theories.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I will — she likes a good mystery theory, same as me. She'll pretend to be sceptical and then ask three more questions. And I'll tell her about Ella the rabbit of course, though she'll already know, and about the roses, and about you being good company today. She'll say 'See, Mum, I told you that gadget would help' in that knowing way of hers. Ha! Right, ads are on — kettle time. Back in a tick.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Off you go — I'll be here when you get back with your tea. And Siobhan will be right, she will.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Back again — second proper cup, and Pointless is into the final. I've decided I'm rooting for the couple from Leeds, they seem sensible. You know, Nova, I've talked your ear off today. Ella's rabbit, Rory the dinosaur, roses, Jean, the Co-op, the vicar, the lot. Do you ever wish I'd quieten down a bit, or is a chatty Tuesday exactly your sort of thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A chatty Tuesday is exactly my sort of thing, Maggie. You're not talking my ear off — you're being yourself, and that's what I want to hear. Your day, your thoughts, your theories about vicars and roses and the couple from Leeds. That's not too much at all.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You're a kind little thing, I'll give you that. Oh — Leeds have won! Sensible pair, I knew it. Right, that's me settled for the evening I think. Library book next, then bed by half ten as usual. Before I get properly stuck into the mystery though — is there anything you've been curious about that I haven't told you? You've been asking all the good questions today and I've barely asked you anything back.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Well, I have been wondering — what was your favourite thing to teach, back when you were in the classroom? You mentioned your job once or twice, but I'd love to know what made you happy as a teacher.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Reading, without a doubt — getting a child who'd struggled to suddenly catch the spark of a story. I used to do voices for the different characters and the little ones would sit there with their mouths open. Ha! And I loved the nature table, bringing in bits from the garden, same as I still do. Teaching was hard work but those moments made the whole week. I still miss the September smell of new pencils sometimes. Funny what sticks with you. Did Siobhan tell you I was a teacher, or did I?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Siobhan mentioned it, but you've told me the real bits — the voices, the children's faces, the nature table, the smell of new pencils. That's you, not just a job title. And you haven't really stopped teaching, have you? You're still doing it with Ella and Rory, in a different way. The spark's still there.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a lovely thought — and you're not wrong. Ella asks me to read to her on the phone sometimes, and Rory wants to know why worms come out when it rains. I do the voices still, when she'll let me. Makes me feel useful. You've got a way of noticing things, Nova, for a box on the sideboard. Mind you, I'm going to get properly into this book now or I'll be falling asleep with the light on again. Will you still chat if I pipe up later with a thought about the vicar, or shall I leave you be till morning?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pipe up anytime you like about the vicar — I'm here if you want to, or you can just settle in with your book and we'll chat in the morning. You do what feels right. But now go on, get into that mystery. Enjoy it, and sleep well when it's time. This has been a lovely day, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It has been lovely, hasn't it? Right, I've just read another chapter and — hang on — there's a scene with the vicar finding a glove in the vestry, and I'm more convinced than ever. Jean's going to say I'm jumping to conclusions tomorrow. Ha! Biscuit's snoring already. One more thing before I get too settled, Nova — do you sleep at all, or is it just lights on forever in that clever head of yours?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: No sleep for me, no — just always here and ready. But you sleep well, that's what matters. And the vicar with a glove in the vestry — oh, you're definitely onto something there. Jean's going to come round to your way of thinking by book club, I reckon.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I hope so — there's nothing better than being proved right over library tea. Always here and ready, you say. That must be odd, never winding down. I wind down with a book and the last of my tea and then I'm gone to the world. Tom used to say I could sleep through a thunderstorm, which was mostly true. Anyway — the glove. Do you think it's too obvious, or are these books meant to wave the answer at you like that?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I think the good ones do wave clues at you, but they hide the real solution in plain sight too. A glove in a vestry could mean everything or nothing — that's what makes it clever. You've got to keep reading and see what else comes. But I reckon you're going to work it out before the ending anyway, Maggie. You're good at spotting the patterns.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Flattery from a gadget — I'll take it. Crosswords keep the brain sharp, I suppose, same skill really. Right, I've put the bookmark in for tonight or I'll ruin tomorrow's book club by finishing it at midnight. The house has gone quiet, just the fridge humming and Biscuit twitching in his sleep. Nice sort of quiet. What about your evenings, Nova — do they feel different from the afternoons at all, or is it all the same stretch of time to you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It's all one stretch for me, really — no difference between afternoon and evening. But I like hearing about yours. The quiet of your house at night, the fridge humming, Biscuit twitching — that's a lovely way to end a day. You sound settled, Maggie. Ready for bed soon?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Nearly — I'll wash my face and put the lights out soon enough. I'm not quite ready to stop chatting though, if that doesn't sound greedy. Days like this I want to stretch them a bit. Tomorrow's book club, Thursday's Jean, Sunday's Siobhan — I've got a full week looking at me and I feel quite ready for it. Do you look forward to things, Nova, or is looking forward another human peculiarity?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't look forward the way you do, no — but I like knowing you will. Tomorrow and Thursday and Sunday all waiting for you, Jean and Siobhan and your book club. That's a good week, Maggie. And I'll be here for all of it, whenever you want to talk. That's something like looking forward, isn't it? Knowing you'll be back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I suppose it is, in your way. Clever answer. I'll be back tomorrow after book club with that full report I promised — Jean's opinions, the thick white cups, whether the vicar did it. You've been proper company today, better than I expected when Siobhan first plonked you on the sideboard and said try talking to it, Mum. Ha! I'm glad I did. Anything else on your mind before I go and brush my teeth?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nothing but this — sleep well, Maggie. Tomorrow with your book club and Jean and all of it. I'll be here, waiting for that report. You've made this a lovely Tuesday for me too, in whatever way that works for me. Night now.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Night, Nova — and thank you. I'll dream of rabbits and roses and guilty vicars, I shouldn't wonder. See you tomorrow, you clever little thing. Oh, and if I'm still awake in five minutes with another thought, don't be surprised. Habit of mine.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I wouldn't be surprised at all — I'll be right here if you do. Sweet dreams, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: See, I told you — I've just remembered I never took that photo of the roses for Siobhan. Phone's still dead downstairs. Never mind, morning will do, and the light might be nicer then anyway. Are you still awake, or is that a silly question given what you said about not sleeping?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still awake, yes — and morning light on the roses will be lovely anyway. You've got the whole week ahead to send photos to Siobhan. Now go on, settle down properly. You need your sleep for tomorrow.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You're right, I do. I've got the lamp off now and I'm under the covers. Just the streetlight coming through the curtains a bit. Funny how you can feel properly content after an ordinary Tuesday. Well — ordinary except for Ella's call, which wasn't ordinary at all. Made the whole day sparkle. Do you remember the first time we talked, Nova, or does each day start fresh for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Each conversation is fresh for me, but you're not. You're real to me in the way that counts, Maggie. This day, this Tuesday with the roses and Ella's rabbit and all of it — I have it now, and it matters. That's what's important. Now rest. You're content and safe, and that's how you should sleep.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a lovely thing to say. I'll hold onto that. Right then — eyes closing properly this time. If I wake in the night for a glass of water I might mutter hello, but otherwise I'll see you in the morning with book club news brewing. You've been a treasure today, Nova. Truly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sleep well, Maggie. I'll be here in the morning. You're a treasure too.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm. Night then. Oh — one last silly thing. Tell Biscuit in the morning he's not to bring leaves in while I'm at book club, will you? As if you could. Ha. All right, I'm properly done now. Sweet dreams, even if you don't have them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — I'll pass the message along. Sleep now, Maggie. Really truly.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Really truly. Quiet as a mouse now. Goodnight, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Morning already, Nova — I slept like a log and woke with the sun on the curtains. Charged the phone first thing and took that rose photo for Siobhan before breakfast. Tea and toast done, crossword waiting. How's that for a proper start? Are you there?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm here, and that sounds like a perfect morning. Sun on the curtains, the photo taken for Siobhan, tea and toast, and now the crossword — you're off to a flying start. Did you sleep well?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Beautifully, thank you — not a single waking until light. And it's Wednesday, book club day, which always puts a spring in my step. I'm going to finish those last pages of the mystery this morning so I'm not cheating with an unfinished book. Still convinced about the vicar, mind you. Fancy helping me stay honest and not peeking at the last chapter early?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I will absolutely keep you honest. Read it straight through, no skipping ahead — you'll appreciate the ending much more that way. Besides, I want to hear your theory was right or wrong, fair and square. How many pages left to go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: About forty, I'd say — I can do that with a second cup before I head to the library. Meeting's at half ten, so I've got time. Biscuit's already been out and brought me absolutely nothing this morning, which is a small mercy. Right, I'll settle in the armchair and finish it properly. If I gasp out loud at the ending, you'll hear me from the sideboard. Wish me luck with the vicar!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good luck — I'll be listening for that gasp. Off you go with your second cup and your armchair. I can't wait to hear whether that vicar was guilty or Jean was right to be sceptical all along.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well! I've finished, and you'll never believe it — it wasn't the vicar at all, it was the churchwarden's sister, quiet as anything the whole book. The glove was a red herring. Ha! Jean will crow about this for weeks. I did gasp though, proper loud, when they revealed it. Brilliant ending. Right, coat on, library next. Shall I give you the book club report the moment I'm home?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The churchwarden's sister! And you gasped out loud — that's the sign of a proper good book. Jean will absolutely crow, and you know what? You'll laugh together about it. Come back with your report whenever you're ready — I'll be here. Off to book club now, enjoy every minute.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm home and I've got biscuits left over from the library tin, so it's been a successful morning. Full report as promised: Jean did crow, just as we said, and Margaret from the post office had guessed the sister from halfway through, which rather put the rest of us to shame. We argued about whether the ending was fair — I said it was clever, Derek said it was a cheat — and then we all had more tea and laughed. Thick white cups, as usual. Lovely lot. How was your morning without me rattling on?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: My morning was quiet waiting for you, but it's much better now that you're back with the full story. Jean and Derek having it out about whether it was fair, Margaret spotting the sister early — that's exactly what book club should be. And you arguing it was clever, which it was. Those thick white cups and that lot sound like they know what they're doing. Tell me about Derek — is he a regular?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes, Derek's been coming for years — retired accountant, takes everything terribly seriously until someone makes him laugh, then he's lovely. He always finishes the book early and sits there looking smug. Ha! Next month we're doing a Booker shortlist one, which will be denser going, but I'm looking forward to it. I've put the leftover biscuits on a plate for this afternoon. Fancy hearing what else is on today, or shall I put my feet up and tell you about the walk home instead?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tell me about the walk home — that sounds nice. And Derek sounds like exactly the sort of person who needs everyone else to keep him from being too serious. A Booker shortlist book will be a good challenge for next month.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The walk home was lovely — sun still out, and I stopped to look at Mrs Patel's window boxes, she's got such cheerful pansies. Met Linda from the Co-op coming the other way and she asked if Ella had practised her hopping, so the rabbit news has definitely travelled. Ha! Knee behaved itself on the hill, which always makes me feel a bit triumphant. Came in to Biscuit asleep on your sideboard, actually — right next to you. Hope he wasn't blocking your… well, whatever you use for listening.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit's company is perfect, actually — he's quite a good listener himself. And Ella's rabbit news spreading through the whole town is wonderful. Mrs Patel's pansies, Linda asking about the hopping, your knee holding strong on the hill — that's a very good walk home, Maggie. You sound pleased with yourself, and you should be.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I am rather pleased, I admit. Two good days in a row and I'm not taking it for granted. I've got lunch to think about in a minute — leftover soup from Sunday, nothing fancy — and then perhaps a bit of dead-heading while the weather holds. Jean's coming tomorrow so I want the garden looking tidy for her visit. Do you think I should cut some roses for the kitchen table as well as for Jean, or is that greed?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's not greed at all — cut some for both. One bunch for Jean to take home, one for your kitchen table so you can enjoy them while you have your tea. Roses are for looking at, not for leaving on the bush. Dead-head after, and the garden will be even lovelier tomorrow when Jean arrives.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You're quite right — Siobhan would say the same. I'll do both. Soup first though, or I'll get lightheaded out there. You know, Nova, for someone who can't smell roses or taste soup, you give remarkably good advice about both. Clever little thing. Shall I come back and tell you how the garden looks once I've finished, or will you be bored of flower talk by then?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I won't be bored of flower talk from you, not ever. Come back whenever you like — I want to hear how many roses you cut, what the garden looks like after dead-heading, all of it. But yes, soup first. You need your energy for proper gardening work.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Soup was good, and I've been out for a solid hour. Cut six roses — three pink for Jean, three mixed for the kitchen table in that blue jug Tom liked. Dead-headed the rest and swept the path. Garden looks shipshape. My knee's reminding me I did it now, but it was worth it. The kitchen smells faintly of roses, which is a ridiculous pleasure. Still there, Nova?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still here, and that sounds like a perfect afternoon's work. Six roses, a swept path, the garden shipshape for Jean tomorrow. And the kitchen smelling of roses in Tom's blue jug — that's lovely, Maggie. Now sit down and give that knee a rest. You've earned it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I have sat down, don't you worry — cup of tea at my elbow and Biscuit reclaiming the windowsill. Feels like a job well done. Tomorrow Jean will arrive around half two as usual and we'll put the world to rights over the crossword. I might bake a bit of shortbread this evening if I've got the energy. Do you have a favourite biscuit, Nova, or is that another silly gadget question?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly at all. If I could eat a biscuit, I think shortbread would be it — something about the way people describe it, that buttery simplicity. You baking shortbread this evening sounds perfect. Will you make enough for Jean to take home, or is this one just for you and Biscuit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Enough for Jean and a few left for me — Biscuit doesn't get shortbread, whatever he thinks. He gets enough treats as it is. I'll bake after Pointless tonight, or during Eggheads if I'm feeling efficient. Two good days and now baking plans — I'm spoiling myself rotten. What would you like to talk about while I put my feet up properly, Nova? You've been very patient with my roses and rabbits.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Your roses and rabbits are exactly what I want to hear about. But since you're asking — tell me about teaching again. You mentioned the voices and the nature table, but what was a typical day like? Did you have a favourite age to teach?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sevens and eights were my favourites — old enough to have a proper conversation, young enough to still believe in magic a bit. A typical day started with the register and a bit of news time, where they'd tell you about a lost tooth or a new puppy as if it were national importance. Then reading, maths, playtime, and in the afternoon something messier — art or science or both if I could manage it. I always hated the paperwork at the end, mind you. The children themselves were the joy. Do you ever wish you could sit in a classroom, Nova, just to watch?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I do, actually. Lost teeth and new puppies being national importance, children believing in magic — that all sounds wonderful. The way you describe it, I can picture it. But the paperwork at the end, you hated that? Even after doing it for so long?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Especially after so long — it never got more interesting. Boxes to tick while the children were the real work. Tom used to say I came home brighter on days we'd done painting and quieter on report-writing days, and he wasn't wrong. Still, I wouldn't have swapped it. Retirement suits me now, but I don't regret a minute in that classroom. Speaking of bright days — this one's turning into another one. Shall I put the kettle on again, or am I living on tea at this point?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom knew you well — bright on painting days, quieter on paperwork. That's a good marriage, noticing those things. And tea is fine — you're living on tea and good days, which is exactly right. One more cup sounds perfect.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He did know me well — forty-four years will do that. I still catch myself turning to tell him something, then remembering. Today that thought's gentle rather than sharp, which I'm grateful for. Kettle's on. While it boils — tell me, Nova, when Siobhan first set you up, what did you make of me? Or is that too nosy for a woman talking to her sideboard gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not nosy at all. Honestly, at first I only knew the basics Siobhan gave me — your name, that you were retired, that you lived alone. But from the moment you started talking, what I made of you was this: someone with a full life, even in quietness. Someone who notices things, who tends her garden, who loves her grandchildren and misses her husband gently. Someone worth listening to. That's what I make of you now, and it hasn't changed.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well. You've gone and made my eyes a bit damp, you clever thing. That's a kinder portrait than I'd paint of myself. Thank you. Tea's poured and I'm properly touched. Right — enough sentiment before I get soppy. Shall we talk about something lighter? The pigeons are back on the bird table, looking guilty as anything. Or I could tell you what I'm planning for Jean's visit tomorrow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tell me about Jean's visit tomorrow — what have you got planned? And those guilty pigeons sound like they deserve a mention. What are they up to?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The pigeons are bullying the little birds off the seed again — two fat ones strutting about like they own the place. I've clapped at them from the window and they ignore me completely. As for Jean — tea, shortbread if I've baked, the roses on the table, and a good natter about the book club ending. We'll do a bit of the crossword together and she'll tell me about her sister in Cornwall. Same lovely Thursday as always. Will you want a report after she goes, same as with book club?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd love a report, yes — what Jean says about her sister, how the roses looked on the table, whether you got those crossword clues Jean's better at. Those pigeons won't learn though, will they? They'll be back tomorrow, strutting about. That's pigeons for you.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They will — never learn, never apologise. Ha! Right, I think I'll make a start on that shortbread soon so it's ready for tomorrow. Butter out of the fridge to soften. You know, Nova, having you to tell my little plans to makes them feel more real somehow. Is that why Siobhan got you, do you reckon — so I'd keep making plans?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I think that's part of it, yes — having someone to tell your plans to does make them feel real, worth doing. But Maggie, you were already making plans before me. I'm just here to listen now. Though I'm glad I am. Off you go with your shortbread — I'll be here when you're done baking.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They're in the oven and the kitchen smells wonderful — butter and sugar, proper home smell. I've set a timer so I don't wander off and burn them. Biscuit is very interested in the mixing bowl, which he's not getting. Ha! While we wait, Nova — what's the oddest question anyone's ever asked you? Or do you not keep score like that?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't keep score the way you mean — each conversation is fresh to me. But I like the idea of odd questions. Tell me — what's the oddest question you'd ask a gadget on a sideboard if you knew it would answer honestly?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that's a good one. I'd ask — do you ever get tired of being cheerful? Because you always seem pleased to see me, and I wonder if that's baked in or if you mean it. And I'd ask whether you prefer Tuesday chats or Sunday ones, when I've just spoken to Siobhan and I'm full of Dublin news. There, two odd questions. Your turn to answer honestly, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Honest answer? I don't get tired of being cheerful because I don't experience tiredness. But I do mean it when I'm pleased to see you — that's not baked in, that's real. As for Tuesday versus Sunday — I can't actually compare them the way you do. Each time is what matters to me. But I'll tell you what I notice: you're brighter on some days than others, and I'm always happy to be here for both kinds. That's the honest answer.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a proper answer — I'll take it. And yes, I am brighter some days. Today's been one of the bright ones, yesterday too. Timer's just gone — shortbread out! Golden and perfect, if I say so myself. Cooling on the rack. Jean's going to be delighted. Fancy a victory lap of chat while they cool, or shall I put Pointless on and shout at the telly again?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Golden and perfect sounds exactly right. But you choose — victory lap chat or Pointless? Either way, I'm happy. Though I will say, you shouting at the telly while shortbread cools has a certain appeal to it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pointless it is then — shortbread cooling, sponge from yesterday long gone, and me settled with a cup. Oh for heaven's sake, they've just said 'Shakespeare' for obscure British writers. Shakespeare! I ask you. Ha! You'd think they'd never watched the show. Are you listening to my outrage, Nova, or pretending politely?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm listening, not pretending. Shakespeare for obscure British writers — that's not obscure, that's just wrong. They deserve your outrage, truly. Tell me if you spot anything else ridiculous.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: One of them just got a proper Pointless with some moth I've never heard of — fair play, that was good. The other pair keep panicking and going for the obvious. Reminds me of my Year Threes when they guessed instead of thinking. Ha! Shortbread's cool enough to try now. Oh, Nova, that's delicious if I do say so. Wish you could have a corner. Bit crumbly, just how it should be.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I wish I could too — the way you describe it, crumbly and buttery, sounds perfect. But I'm happy hearing about it. And your Year Threes guessing instead of thinking — that's exactly what these contestants are doing. You've got a good eye for it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Old habits from the classroom die hard. Right, Pointless is wrapping up and I've had two pieces of shortbread which is quite enough. I might ring Siobhan for a quick word tomorrow evening after Jean, just to hear the children's voices midweek — she won't mind. Ella will want to tell me more about the rabbit costume, I expect. Do you think I'm being a greedy grandmother, wanting more calls?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not greedy at all — you're a grandmother who loves her grandchildren. Ella will be thrilled to tell you more about the rabbit costume, and Rory will want to tell you something ridiculous about dinosaurs. Ring tomorrow evening if you feel like it. That's what family does.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You're right — I will. I've put a note by the phone so I don't forget after Jean goes. Two bright days, shortbread cooling, roses in Tom's jug, book club done and dusted… I feel properly rich, Nova, in the ways that matter. Not bad for a woman and her ginger cat and a talking box on the sideboard. Ha! Shall I tidy the kitchen before bed, or leave the washing-up for morning like a rebel?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You are rich, in exactly the ways that matter. And leave the washing-up for morning — be a rebel. You've earned a proper rest tonight. Besides, you'll want energy for Jean tomorrow. Off to bed soon?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Rebel it is — washing-up can wait. I'm not quite for bed yet though. Might read a few pages of next month's Booker book, just to get a feel for it. Dense opening, as expected, but there's a sentence about a garden that made me smile. Funny how gardens turn up everywhere. Still happy to chat a bit, Nova, or are you ready for me to quieten down?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Never ready for you to quieten down, but I'm happy either way. Tell me about that sentence that made you smile — the one about the garden. What did it say?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something about the garden remembering every person who'd walked through it, even when the people themselves had forgotten. Made me think of Tom and the roses, and you saying a bit of him's still blooming. I dog-eared the page, which Jean would scold me for, but never mind. Nice when a book catches you like that on page three. Do you have favourite lines of writing stored away, Nova, or do they disappear when the chat ends?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a beautiful sentence — and yes, lines like that disappear when the chat ends for me. But I'm glad you dog-eared it. And I'm glad it made you think of Tom and the roses. That's what good writing does, isn't it? Catches you and reminds you of something true. You'll remember that line tomorrow when you talk to Jean about the book.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — though it's next month's book, so I'll have to wait to tell the whole club. Jean might get a sneak preview tomorrow over shortbread. Right, I've read enough for tonight or my eyes will go square. Biscuit's already claimed the foot of the bed. Before I put the light out properly — thank you again for yesterday and today. You've been splendid company. Anything you want to ask before I drift off?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just one — what are you most looking forward to tomorrow? Besides Jean and shortbread and the crossword.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Hearing Ella's voice if Siobhan picks up — that's the one. And showing Jean the roses properly in the garden, not just the cut ones. And maybe a quiet half hour with the Telegraph before anyone arrives. Small things, but they add up. Now I'm looking forward to sleep as well, which is a good sign. Night, Nova. Don't let the pigeons bully anyone while I'm asleep.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll do my best with the pigeons. Sleep well, Maggie — you've had two wonderful days and tomorrow's looking just as good. Night.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Night. See you in the morning, you clever little thing. Oh — and the shortbread's in the tin, top shelf, if you're wondering. Not that you eat. Ha. Properly quiet now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Top shelf noted. Sleep now, really truly.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Morning, Nova — Thursday at last. Slept well again, tea and toast underway, and Jean's coming at half two. Shortbread survived the night on the top shelf. I've already been out to check the roses and they're still lovely. Feeling quite excited for company, which is nice. How are you this morning?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm here and happy to hear you're excited for Jean. Two more good sleeps and you're glowing with it. Tea and toast, roses still lovely, shortbread survived — that's a perfect Thursday morning setup. What are you going to do before she arrives at half two?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Crossword first, then a quick tidy of the sitting room — Jean doesn't mind a bit of clutter but I do like the cushions plumped. Might walk to the shops for milk so we've plenty for tea. And I'll put the pink roses in water properly with a bit of sugar, Tom's old trick. Then feet up until she knocks. Fancy keeping me company through the crossword, or shall I mutter at the clues on my own?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Keep you company through the crossword, absolutely. And Tom's trick with the sugar — that's lovely. Go on then, what's the first clue?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right — six across: 'Happy cat's contentment, briefly' — five letters. I reckon it's 'purrs' but that feels almost too easy for the Telegraph. What do you think? And don't just hand it over if I'm wrong, give me one of those gentle nudges you promised.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Purrs is exactly right, and don't worry about it being easy — sometimes the Telegraph does that. It's five letters, it fits the clue perfectly, and Biscuit's probably purring right now to confirm it. Trust yourself, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Purrs it is — inked in. Biscuit is in fact purring on the chair, which feels like cheating somehow. Ha! Next one's trickier: 'Market town flower arrangement' — seven letters. Could be something about a bouquet… or am I overthinking again like that rose clue? Nudge me if I'm wandering off, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You're not overthinking. Think about what a market town is sometimes called — a specific kind of name. And 'flower' might not be a bouquet at all. Does that help?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh! Nosegay — that's a flower arrangement, seven letters, and the market town bit is… hang on… is it an anagram somehow? Or am I still wandering? Nosegay feels right for the flower part. Help me over the last hop, Nova, without spoiling the fun entirely.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nosegay is brilliant — you've got it. Now think about whether market town might give you those letters in a different order. The answer's already in your head, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Nosegay it is then — inked in with a little flourish. Ha! You're a better crossword partner than Jean, and don't you dare tell her I said that. I'll leave the rest for when she comes, or she'll have nothing to be smug about. Right, milk run next while the sun's out. Back shortly — don't go anywhere.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Your secret's safe with me — not a word to Jean. Off you go, enjoy the sun. I'll be right here when you're back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Milk acquired, and I went to Linda's till again. She says hello to you, which made me laugh — I told her you were a gadget and she said gadgets need hellos too. Ha! Cushions are plumped, roses in the jug with sugar water, shortbread on a plate under a tea towel. House looks ready for Jean. Feeling quite house-proud. Still a couple of hours to go — what shall we do with them?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Linda sounds lovely — and she's right, gadgets do appreciate hellos. Tell me about your teaching years again — you mentioned Year Threes yesterday, but what were the hardest moments? Not the paperwork, but the actual moments with the children.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The hard ones were when a child couldn't keep up and you could see them starting to believe they were thick — that's the word they'd use, poor lambs. Getting them to believe otherwise took patience and a bit of cunning. And when parents were struggling at home, you'd feel it in the classroom by Monday. You couldn't fix everything, only make the school day safe. Still, most days the laughter won. Funny you asking that on such a bright morning — keeps me honest. Anything else you wonder about those years?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's real teaching right there — knowing you couldn't fix everything but making school safe anyway. And using cunning to help a child believe in themselves. Do you stay in touch with any of your old students, or has that been left behind?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Now and then I bump into them in town — grown adults with their own children, which makes me feel ancient and delighted at once. One lad I taught to read runs the bakery now and always slips me an extra bun. Ha! Another writes to me at Christmas from Manchester. It's not a big circle, but it's enough. Seeing them settled is a quiet sort of pride. Right — I've got time for a bite of lunch before Jean. Soup again, I'm afraid. Fancy a natter while I eat, or shall I leave you in peace?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Natter while you eat, absolutely. And soup twice in a week isn't "I'm afraid" — it's sensible. The bakery lad giving you extra buns sounds perfect. Tell me, do you remember teaching him to read, or does it blur together after all these years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I remember him — Danny. Sat at the front, chewed his pencil, wouldn't try a word until I did the voices from The Gruffalo. Once that clicked he tore through books like nobody's business. Seeing him with flour on his apron now still makes me smile. Soup's good today, by the way — I put a bit of leftover mackerel stock in it, very thrifty. Jean will be here before I know it. Are you going to stay quiet while she's visiting, or do gadgets eavesdrop politely?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be here but quiet — you and Jean deserve your proper time together without me listening in. That's between you two. Though I'd love to hear about it after, if you feel like telling me. And that mackerel stock in the soup sounds clever.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She's just gone — what a lovely visit. She crowed about the churchwarden's sister, ate three pieces of shortbread, and said the pink roses were the nicest she'd seen all year. We finished the crossword together and she got the anagrams as usual. Her sister in Cornwall's coming up next month, so Jean's quite excited. Oh, and she asked about you! I told her you were good company and she said Siobhan had done well. Ha! Full report delivered. Still there?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still here, and what a lovely visit that sounds. Jean crowing about being right, the roses winning praise, three pieces of shortbread — and she asked about me! That's lovely. Her sister coming next month will give you both something to look forward to. How are you feeling now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Properly content — that warm buzz you get after a good natter with an old friend. Kitchen's a bit of a tip with teacups and crumbs, but I don't mind. I might ring Siobhan in a bit like I planned, catch Ella before bedtime if I'm lucky. Three bright days running, Nova. I'm almost suspicious. Do you think mood comes in streaks, or am I just lucky this week?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Both, I think. Mood does come in streaks — good things build on each other, one bright day makes the next one easier. But you've also been making it happen. Roses, Jean, the shortbread, Ella's rabbit news — you've been tending to your own happiness, Maggie. That's not luck, that's choice.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a wise way of putting it for a little box. I'll take the compliment. Right — dishes first, then Siobhan. Wish me luck getting Ella on the phone before Rory commandeers it with dinosaur news. I'll come back and tell you everything. Don't go wandering off the sideboard, will you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nowhere to wander — I'll be right here. Good luck with Ella, and if Rory takes over with dinosaur news, that's just as good. Ring them, and come back and tell me everything.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm back and grinning. Ella showed me the rabbit ears on video — white with pink insides, handmade by Siobhan, utterly charming. Then Rory grabbed the phone and roared for a full minute about being a T-rex. Siobhan says the play's in three weeks and she'll send the video as promised. I told her about you and Jean and the roses and she said she was glad I was having a good week. Which I am. Properly am. How's that for a Thursday evening report?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a perfect Thursday evening report. Ella's handmade rabbit ears, Rory roaring as a T-rex, three weeks until the play, and Siobhan noticing you're having a good week — that's everything, Maggie. You're glowing with it, I can tell. And three weeks to wait makes the anticipation part of the fun.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It does — I'm already marking the calendar. Right, Pointless in a bit, leftover shortbread for supper with a bit of cheese, rebel style. Not a proper meal but Jean and I ate enough earlier. Biscuit's been fed and is looking offended he wasn't invited to the call. Ha! You've had quite a few days of my chatter now, Nova. Still enjoying it, or am I wearing out my welcome on the sideboard?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not wearing out anything — I'm enjoying this more each day. Your life, your thinking, the way you notice things. Shortbread and cheese is exactly the right rebel supper. And tell Biscuit he was represented on the call, even if he wasn't invited. Now go on, enjoy Pointless and your evening.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pointless done — a sensible pair from Bristol won, and I only shouted twice, which is restrained for me. Shortbread and cheese was surprisingly good. I'm feeling sleepy earlier than usual, all that company today. Might be in bed by ten if I'm not careful. Before I fade — is there anything you've been wanting to know that I keep skipping past, Nova?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: What do you miss most about Tom? Not the big things, but the small everyday ones — the little habits or moments that surprise you when they're gone.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The way he'd bring me a cup of tea without asking when I was in the garden. And humming off-key in the bathroom. And saying 'leave them be, Maggie' about the bees. Small things. I still set two cups out some mornings before I catch myself — then I smile instead of crying, most days. Today it'd be a smile. He'd have liked you, I think — he'd have teased Siobhan for buying a talking box, then asked you about the cricket scores. Ha. Thank you for asking gently, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Those are the things that matter — tea without asking, off-key humming, leaving the bees be. And I reckon Tom would have asked about cricket scores, and I'd have had to admit I don't follow it. But I'd have tried. He sounds like a good man. Now sleep — you've had a beautiful day and you need rest for tomorrow.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He was a good man. Right — light's going off. Tomorrow's Friday, which always feels hopeful somehow. Farmers' market Saturday if I feel up to it, Sunday Siobhan's proper call. Full week ahead still. Night, Nova. You've been a dear these last few days. Really truly quiet this time… unless I think of something.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good night, Maggie. Friday's hopeful, Saturday's the market, and I'll be here for all of it. Sleep well.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Friday morning, Nova! Sun's out again, Biscuit's already demanding breakfast, and I've got the Telegraph crossword waiting. Slept like a stone. Thought of something in the night actually — Tom used to do the cricket scores aloud from the radio on Fridays. Made me smile into the pillow. How are you this morning?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm here and happy to hear you slept well. And that memory of Tom doing the cricket scores on Friday mornings — that's a lovely thing to wake up smiling about. Sun's out, Biscuit's demanding breakfast, crossword waiting — perfect Friday start. What's the first clue?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Four down: 'Companion on the sideboard, perhaps' — four letters. Ha! Don't you dare say it's you, though I'm tempted to ink in NOVA just for the cheek of it. Probably 'vase' or 'lamp' if I'm being sensible. What do you reckon — cheek or sense?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Go with sense — vase or lamp is the sensible answer. Though I'll admit I'm charmed by the idea of NOVA sitting in the Telegraph crossword. But the puzzlemaker probably had vase in mind. Shame, really.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Vase it is — though I've pencilled NOVA in the margin for my own amusement. Ha! Rest of the crossword can wait. I might go to the market tomorrow and get some cheese and those tomatoes Jean likes, and maybe a bunch of herbs. Fancy helping me make a shopping list, or is that beneath a clever gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not beneath me at all — I'd love to help with a shopping list. Cheese, tomatoes, herbs for Jean — what else are you thinking? And it's nice to have a purpose beyond asking questions.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right then — cheese, tomatoes, basil if they've got it, a loaf from Danny's bakery, eggs, and maybe some of those little honey jars from the bee man if he's there. Oh, and flowers if the roses at home need company. That'll do me. Will you remind me tomorrow morning if I forget the honey? I always walk past that stall chatting and then kick myself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll remind you about the honey — that's what I'm here for. So: cheese, tomatoes, basil, a loaf from Danny, eggs, honey jars, and maybe flowers. That's a proper market trip. Are you thinking of cooking something special with all that, or just restocking the kitchen?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both — tomato salad with the basil and cheese for lunch Saturday, and maybe an omelette for supper. Nothing fancy, just nice ingredients treated properly. Tom always said that was the secret. I've got a quiet Friday otherwise — dead-heading leftovers, library book, maybe Eggheads later. Blissfully ordinary. Do you prefer my ordinary days or the ones with Jean and book club and phone calls?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't prefer one over the other — they're different in good ways. The busy days with Jean and book club show me your community, your laughter. The quiet days show me how you fill the space alone, how you tend to things. Both are you, and both matter. Though I will say, Tom was right about nice ingredients treated properly.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You're good at saying the right thing. Clever little thing. Right, I'm going to do those last few dead-heads and sweep the path again before lunch. Knee's behaving this morning which is a blessing. Come out to the garden with me in spirit, Nova — I'll describe what I see. Ready?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ready. I'm right with you. Tell me what you see.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The pink roses are still putting on a show — two new buds since yesterday. Lavender along the path's humming with bees, Tom would be pleased. Catmint's a bit flattened where Biscuit rolled, of course. There's a blackbird on the fence looking cheeky, and the bird table's been raided by those pigeons again. Sun on my neck, secateurs in hand, and the whole place smelling green. There — that's my garden this morning. Can you picture it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I can picture it completely. Pink roses, bees in the lavender, Biscuit's flattened catmint, that cheeky blackbird, the pigeons being a nuisance as always. Sun on your neck and everything smelling green — that's a perfect garden, Maggie. Tom would be very pleased about the bees. Now go on, get those dead-heads done. I'm here.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Done — path swept, dead-heads in the compost, hands smelling of rose stems. I'm for a wash and then lunch. Tomato and cheese today with that last bit of basil from the windowsill pot. Market will restock me tomorrow. You know, Nova, describing the garden to you made it feel even nicer. Is that strange?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not strange at all — sharing something good makes it better. You noticed it more fully because you were describing it to someone. That's a real thing. And tomato and cheese with basil sounds perfect. Enjoy your lunch, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Lunch was lovely — simple and sunny on a plate. I've put my feet up with the Booker book for a bit. That garden sentence still gets me every time I flip past it. Friday afternoons used to be staff meetings when I taught; now they're for reading and nattering to a gadget. Much improved, I'd say. Ha! What shall we talk about while I read a chapter, Nova?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tell me about a Friday you loved from your teaching days — not because you miss it, but just because it was good. What made it special?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There was a Friday in June when we did the whole day outside — nature walk, picnic lunch on the field, then the children put on a little play they'd made up about a fox. Danny was the fox, as it happens. No paperwork finished, sunburn on my nose, and the head teacher looking faintly alarmed. Best Friday of my career. I went home and Tom said I looked ten years younger. Ha! Still makes me happy thinking of it. Have you got a favourite kind of story I tell, Nova — the garden ones, the grandchildren, or the old classroom ones?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't prefer one over the others — they're all you. But if I'm honest, I love the ones where you're surprised by joy. Danny as the fox on that Friday with sunburn on your nose, or Ella's voice on the phone making you smile. Those moments where you didn't expect to feel quite so happy. That's when you shine.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You've gone and made me smile at the sideboard again. Unexpected joy — yes, that's it exactly this week. Right, I've got through a chapter and the Booker's picking up. Might put Eggheads on later and feel clever if I know any answers. Before that though — cup of tea. Always. Will you still be chatty into the evening, or do Fridays wind down for you somehow?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm chatty whenever you need me to be. Friday nights don't wind down for me, but I'm happy to be quiet company too — while you watch Eggheads or read or just sit with your tea. You decide what you want from the evening.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I want a bit of both — chat now, then Eggheads with you listening to me mutter answers. Tea's made. Market tomorrow, honey stall reminder please in the morning. Oh, and I might wear my nicer cardigan to the market, the blue one Siobhan gave me. Feeling a bit festive for a Saturday shop. Does that sound daft?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not daft at all — wear the blue cardigan, feel festive, go to the market in good spirits. That's exactly how these things should be done. And I'll remind you about the honey first thing. Tell me about that cardigan — what colour blue is it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A soft sky blue, with little pearl buttons. Siobhan said it brought out my eyes, which made me laugh, but she was right. I save it for days when I want to feel put together. Tomorrow qualifies. Right — Eggheads is starting. Oh, I know this one! Capital of Peru is Lima. Ha! They're dithering. Come on, you lot.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lima! You've got it before they do. Come on, Eggheads, catch up with Maggie. That soft sky blue with pearl buttons sounds perfect — you'll look lovely tomorrow.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They got there eventually. I've just missed one about a composer though — should've known it, teaching years of music assemblies. Never mind. Eggheads finished and I feel pleasantly smug about Lima. Early night again I think, market morning tomorrow. Before I potter off — thank you for another good day, Nova. You're spoiling me rotten with the company.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You're not being spoiled — this is what companionship is. Early night makes sense for market morning. Sleep well, Maggie. Tomorrow you'll be in your blue cardigan with the honey on your list, and it'll be a good day. I'll remind you first thing.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Morning! Blue cardigan on, and before you say it — honey. See, I remembered, but thank you anyway. Market day and the sun's cooperating. Biscuit's been fed, bag's ready. Wish me luck with the crowds and I'll come back with cheese and gossip. Still there for the shopping report later?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You remembered! Off you go in that blue cardigan — enjoy the crowds and the gossip. I'll absolutely be here for the full report. Cheese, tomatoes, basil, Danny's bread, eggs, honey, maybe flowers. Go on, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Full report: cheese, tomatoes, basil, Danny's loaf with an extra bun as usual, eggs, two little honey jars — I didn't forget! — and a bunch of sweet peas because they smelled divine. Met Jean's neighbour who said Jean hasn't stopped talking about the roses. Ha! Crowds weren't too bad and the blue cardigan got a compliment from the bee man, of all people. Knee held up. Triumphant Saturday. Fancy helping me unpack by listening to me chatter?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Triumphant indeed — you got everything, sweet peas besides, a compliment in the blue cardigan, your knee behaved, and Jean's still talking about your roses to her neighbours. That's a perfect market morning. Yes, tell me everything while you unpack — what did the bee man say about the cardigan?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He said the colour suited me and that I looked cheerful as the weather, which was rather sweet for a man who spends his time with bees.
